The stock slid in extended trading. Here's how the company did compared to analysts' estimates, according to LSEG. EPS: $2.10 vs. $1.99 expected Revenue: $114.48 billion vs. $113.39 billion expected Here's how Apple's most important product lines performed: iPhone revenue : $57.58 billion vs. $56.54 billion estimated Mac revenue : $10.79 billion vs. $9.61 billion estimated iPad revenue : $6.23 billion vs. $6.7 billion estimated Other Products revenue : $31.57 billion vs. $31.58 billion estimated Wearables, Home and Accessories revenue : $8.3 billion vs. $9.06 billion estimated Gross margin : 47.9% vs. 47.5% It's Apple's first earnings report since CEO John Ternus took the helm on Sept. 1, succeeding Tim Cook . On the earnings call, Apple said it expects revenue to increase between 7% and 10% on an annual basis in the December quarter, compared to the 6.1% average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. The company's gross margin forecast for the current quarter is 45% to 46%, trailing the 46.3% average estimate. Revenue in the past quarter rose 12% from $102.5 billion a year earlier, Apple said in a statement on Monday. Apple's iPhone revenue in the quarter only included eight days of new iPhone 18 Pro sales. And Apple's new flagship device, the iPhone Duo, didn't hit store shelves until the period was over. Monday's report includes a full quarter of higher-priced Apple products, as the company raised prices across the board in June after it signaled challenges with memory supply and other parts. Apple increased prices on iPhones by $100. The iPhone maker is reckoning with a global memory crunch and a rush for computer components. Apple said on Monday that its memory costs were higher this quarter than in the June period. Still, Ternus said in a statement that Apple had just capped off its "best fiscal year ever." Ternus told CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos that Apple's growth came in spite of supply constraints and foreign exchange headwinds. "I think at this point, with everything we've achieved, it just feels like we've never been more confident that the best is yet to come," Ternus said. Ternus said that Apple "reluctantly" raised prices, which helped it offset component costs. Apple said tariff refunds added 5 cents to earnings per share. He said that Apple's revenue would grow between 7% and 10%. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for 6.1%. Apple said that it expected services sales to rise between 8% and 9%, signaling slowing growth. Parekh also said that gross margin would be between 45% and 46%, lower than in the fourth quarter. — Kif Leswing 2 Hours Ago CEO John Ternus addresses investors and analysts on earnings call for the first time as Apple chief Ternus is leading Apple's quarterly earnings call for the first time. Investors want to know if Apple will offer more AI features through subscriptions or services. Ternus said on Monday that Apple has a "lot of opportunities" for monetization. "One example is on the hardware side, right?" Ternus said. "It offers a compelling reason for upgrading or switching." — Kif Leswing 3 Hours Ago iPhone remains half of Apple's sales Apple remains synonymous with the iPhone, which accounted for just over half of Apple's sales in the quarter. Sales of iPhones jumped over 17%, capping off four quarters of strong growth behind last year's iPhone 17 models. Ternus said industry research firms reported market share gains for Apple during the quarter. — Kif Leswing 3 Hours Ago Slowest growth for services since 2022 Customers at the Apple Music section of the new Apple Inc. store in Mumbai, India, on Tuesday, April 18, 2023. Dhiraj Singh | Bloomberg | Getty Images The company's profitable services business grew less than 10% during the September quarter, the slowest expansion since 2022. The category includes a wide variety of products and subscriptions, including iCloud storage, App Store fees, AppleCare warranties, and licensing revenue from Google for using its search engine on the Safari browser. "We saw strong performance in many service categories, with all-time records in video, cloud services, payment services, and advertising, and a September quarter record in music," Ternus told CNBC. — Kif Leswing 3 Hours Ago Apple capex remains far below hyperscaler spending Compared to its megacap peers, which are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into AI capital expenditures, Apple is a light spender. Shannon Stapleton | Reuters In August, Apple announced a new home product called HomeView that uses AI and a display to show personalized information to multiple users in a family. It's potentially a sign that Apple is going to take its home accessories more seriously under Ternus. headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves after hours: FN, CLX, AAPL, PLTR Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in extended trading. Upwork – Shares of the freelance marketplace surged 10% on the back of a guidance raise. Full-year adjusted earnings are expected to range from $1.45 to $1.47 per share, topping the FactSet consensus of $1.39 per share. Palantir Technologies — Palantir shares were down 2% even after the company's third-quarter earnings topped Wall Street's estimates. Revenue for the period nearly doubled from a year earlier and surpassed $2 billion for the first time. The company's U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, topping U.S. government revenue of $953 million. Palantir is also projecting about $2.65 billion in fourth-quarter revenue and $8.53 billion for full-year 2026. Lattice Semiconductor — The company's stock jumped 8% after Lattice solidly outpaced third-quarter revenue estimates and raised its forecast for the year. The semiconductor designer expects fourth-quarter revenue of between $325 million and $345 million, above the $293 million LSEG consensus estimate, and anticipates it will earn 82 cents to 86 cents per share after adjustments, topping the consensus estimate of 64 cents per share. The Clorox Company — The maker of Clorox Disinfecting Wipes added 2% after fiscal first-quarter results came in ahead of estimates. The company earned $1.55 per share on an adjusted basis on revenue of $1.91 billion. Analysts surveyed by LSEG were looking for $1.07 a share and $1.88 billion. Organic sales growth for the period also topped estimates. On Semiconductor — Shares fell about 2%. On Semiconductor said it would acquire Ferric, a maker of power converters, for $600 million in cash, plus up to $175 million in contingent consideration if certain revenue milestones are reached. Separately, the company said it expects fourth-quarter adjusted earnings in a range of 95 cents to $1.07 per share, while analysts polled by LSEG called for 95 cents per share. Apple — Apple shares were down 2% in extended trading after the consumer tech giant rolled out a disappointing margin forecast and iPad sales in the fiscal fourth quarter missed the Street's estimates. Fabrinet – The provider of advanced optical packaging jumped more than 10% after current-quarter guidance trounced the Street's estimates. Fabrinet sees second-quarter adjusted earnings in a range of $4.77 to $4.92 per share on revenue of $1.6 billion to $1.65 billion. Analysts were looking for $4.43 a share and $1.48 billion, per FactSet. Ibotta — The digital consumer promotions company gained 13% after its fourth-quarter guidance beat analysts' expectations. Ibotta sees revenue in a range of $94 million to $98 million, beating the FactSet consensus estimate of $93.4 million. Adjusted EBITDA also topped expectations. CNBC's Deena Zaidi, Scott Schnipper, Christina Cheddar Berk and Nick Wells contributed reporting. headlines.article_text: Palantir (PLTR) earnings Q3 2026 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Palantir reported Q3 earnings that topped Wall Street's estimates. U.S. commercial revenue more than doubled and surpassed U.S. government revenue for the first time. The company has seen a boost from heightened demand for artificial intelligence tools. In this article PLTR Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 1:24 01:24 Palantir beats on earnings and revenue, Q3 commercial revenue surpasses government revenue Closing Bell: Overtime Palantir beat Wall Street's third-quarter estimates after the bell on Monday, with U.S. commercial revenue topping government for the first time as businesses adopt more of the company's artificial intelligence tools. Shares dipped about 3% in extended trading. Here's how the company did compared to LSEG estimates: Earnings per share : 44 cents adjusted vs. 41 cents expected Revenue : $2.31 billion vs. $2.18 billion expected Revenue nearly doubled from a year ago and blew past $2 billion for the first time ever, Palantir said. Net income more than doubled to $1.13 billion, or 44 cents per share, from about $476 million, or 18 cents per share. "I don't believe anyone's had consistent results like this in the history of software AI, ever," CEO Alex Karp told CNBC's Seema Mody in an interview, adding that the business is succeeding without salespeople. Palantir has long been known for its strength in the government sector, but its commercial segment caught up in Q3. U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, surpassing U.S. government revenue of $953 million, which was up 96%. The company's U.S. commercial revenue has more than quintupled over the last two years. Palantir lifted its guidance, saying it now expects U.S. commercial revenue "in excess of" $3.56 billion for the full year. Last quarter, the company boosted its forecast to $3.42 billion. The company projects about $2.65 billion in revenue for the fourth quarter and about $8.53 billion for full-year 2026. Karp has openly supported the use of open-weight models and criticized leading AI labs, which he told CNBC earlier this year are forcing businesses to sell their data sovereignty. Karp, on Monday, also reiterated recent calls to nationalize AI labs, calling it the "only realistic way" to manage liability. In September, Karp joined major tech CEOs at the White House as calls for regulation mounted following claims from AI researchers that the technology has a more than 10% of killing humanity . "My message to everybody is: Beware of thinking you can delay the future in AI," he told CNBC. "The future is here. The political ramifications of it are here." Palantir stock chart.
